subject: Darker thriller and horror subgenres
searchNote: WebSearch summaries were the only web source (WebFetch cannot resolve hosts here). Summaries quoted Wikipedia, publisher and library catalogue pages, Britannica and similar; no primary scans were read.

corrected.was: psychological and domestic suspense commonly run about 70,000 to 90,000 words, a little shorter than other thrillers
corrected.now: Length varies by publisher: roughly 70,000 to 100,000 words, with about 80,000 to 90,000 a frequent target
corrected.why: Search found blog and genre-guide figures of 70,000 to 100,000 and a publisher call of 70,000 to 120,000; nothing supported 'shorter than other thrillers' (spy and general thriller guides give 80,000 to 100,000). The facet is already confidence 'varies'.

Collins, The Woman in White, serialised 1859 to 1860 in All the Year Round

corrected.was: The Thirty-Nine Steps (1915) and Greenmantle (1916) set an adventurous amateur against enemy agents in the First World War.
corrected.now: The Thirty-Nine Steps (1915), set just before the First World War, and Greenmantle (1916) set an adventurous amateur against enemy agents.
corrected.why: Search sources say The Thirty-Nine Steps is set just before the war; only Greenmantle is a wartime Hannay novel. Also trimmed 'quiet' from the Maugham clause to stay within the 300-character limit.

softened.was: The Call of Cthulhu (1928) and At the Mountains of Madness (1936) set people before beings that do not notice them.
softened.now: set people against beings and ages that dwarf them.
softened.why: In At the Mountains of Madness the shoggoths rebel and pursue the explorers, so 'do not notice them' overstated it.

softened.was: Thomas Ligotti's Songs of a Dead Dreamer in 1986, which gave the mode a bleaker, more philosophical turn.
softened.now: Thomas Ligotti's Songs of a Dead Dreamer in the mid-1980s; his work gave the mode a bleaker, more philosophical turn. (Also 'role-playing game' shortened to 'game' for the length limit.)
softened.why: Sources disagree: Wikipedia gives the Silver Scarab Press first edition as 1985 and another listing says it appeared in March 1986. The claim that this one book gave the turn was widened to his work.

softened.was: Thomas Ligotti's Songs of a Dead Dreamer (1986)
softened.now: Thomas Ligotti's Songs of a Dead Dreamer (mid-1980s)

softened.was: The King in Yellow (1895) linked tales around a play that harms those who read it.
softened.now: The King in Yellow (1895) opens with linked tales around a play that harms those who read it.
softened.why: Only the first four stories of the collection are tied to the play; the rest are unrelated.

remainingDoubts: The library's own core entry (knowledge/library/enrich/core-genres.js) still lists Songs of a Dead Dreamer as 1986; that file is outside this task, and the date there is disputed (1985 or March 1986).
S. T. Joshi's biographies being standard Lovecraft scholarship rests on recall; search did not return it (his two-volume I Am Providence appeared in 2010).

The attribution of the Cthulhu Mythos label to Derleth follows Wikipedia and a review; scholarly discussion of whether Lovecraft used a similar phrase was not examined, so the text says 'most associated with', which is hedged.
The 70,000 to 90,000 word figure for horror novels comes from a blog source, not a publisher standard; the facet is confidence 'varies'.
